Remote: Yes - remote only

Willing to relocate: No

Technologies: TypeScript, React, Next.js, Node.js, Fastify, Python, Rust, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, Docker. Agent work: Claude Code, Cursor, MCP, Anthropic + OpenAI APIs, agent orchestration, evaluation harnesses. Also Shopify (Python connectors, inventory and placement CRUD), Solidity/Solana.

Resume: https://www.ayushbaluni.in GitHub: https://github.com/aayushbaluni LinkedIn: https://linkedin.com/in/ayush-baluni Email: abaluni6@gmail.com

I build AI agents that ship real code, and I own the review of everything they produce.

The evidence: I wrote an agent that finds actionable issues in open-source repos, writes the patch, and opens the PR. 17 of those are merged into third-party projects - langflow, dify, Grafana, Flowise, twenty, agno, Directus, pnpm, Medusa, Haystack, windmill, Effect, logto, reth, supabase-js, graph-node and Temporal's TypeScript SDK. Around 726,000 stars combined, all merged between March and July 2026.

Getting a patch past a maintainer who has no reason to be generous to you is the hard part, and it is the part I would point at. The agent does not fail at writing code - it fails at judgment: which issue is actually fixable, when a green test suite is lying, when a one-line fix is really an API change.

Also built Agent Vault, a runtime safety layer for AI agents (Rust, gRPC, NATS) with SHA-256 state verification and a four-tier escalation policy. Day job is product engineering; 15+ freelance projects delivered end to end; CodeChef global rank #22.

Looking for part-time contract work - roughly 15-20 hrs/week, IST with several hours of European or US-East overlap. Most interested in agent infrastructure, evals and developer tooling, but good full-stack product work is welcome too.

comment_text.value:
Finding a tech geek who can put together a coherent sentence is hard, and there are always manuals to write, tutorials to create and deep blog posts to make -- many of which need the kind of in-depth understanding that only a tech geek can bring.

It doesn't always need a technical background -- a friend of mine found a job writing drug trial instructions even though she had no background in medicine or biology. But she was pretty exceptional, and very quick on the up-take so she probably absorbed a couple of years of medtech education in the first few months she was there.

So yes, you can make a career out of that. Apply for jobs and say "I want a role where I can program 50% of the time and write all your public-facing words the other 50% of your time". There are many employers who would pay a premium for that unique combination of skills which you have already demonstrated.

As for freelance authoring... I'm writing book #8 now. The first 6 are all deeply technical books on backup and managing IT (http://www.ifost.org.au/books/ ); the seventh was a collection of mathematics/computing/physics poetry ( http://www.ifost.org.au/books/outlinks/medusa ).

These are rather small niches, but in most of these areas I'm one of the leading experts in the field -- usually because there's no-one else writing anything.

Based on what I'm getting from my work so far, I'd estimate that I would need to get to 50-100 books written before I could stop relying on other sources of income. I live in an expensive city and have a family, so you might be able to do slightly more easily than me. Also, if I wrote something less niche, I might have a bigger market (but probably face more competition).

In other words, I might be able to write full-time in 10-15 years' time if I keep up the current output. That is something I am aiming to do, but it's obviously not a short-term goal.

story_title.value: Ask HN: Is it possible to live off technical writing?

One take-away: At the very least, each school library schould provide:

• Douglas R. Hofstadter, Gödel, Escher, Bach: An Eternal Golden Braid

• David Goodsell, The Machinery of Life

• William W. Cohen, A Computer Scientist’s Guide to Cell Biology

• Horace Freeland Judson, The Eighth Day of Creation: Makers of the Revolution in Biology

• Lewis Thomas, The Medusa and the Snail: More Notes of a Biology Watcher
